title: The word on the tip of the tongue
text: You know the name. You know its {{1}} letter, how many syllables it has, roughly what it sounds like — but the word itself will not {{2}}. This is the tip-of-the-tongue state, and it {{3}} about twice a week for the average adult, more often for bilinguals and for everyone over sixty. It is revealing precisely because the retrieval fails {{4}}: the meaning arrives, the sound does not. Psychologists therefore {{5}} the mental dictionary as partly split — a store of meanings separate from a store of pronunciations — and the tip-of-the-tongue state as the gap between the two {{6}} open at the worst moment. The state is also stubbornly {{7}}: willpower does not help, and the word usually arrives later, when you are thinking of something {{8}} entirely. Attempts to force it produce more wrong candidates than right ones. The practical advice is to stop, let the search quietly continue in the background, and enjoy the small proof that your mind contains far more than your attention can reach.

gaps.explanation: 'its first letter' — the one it starts with; foremost = most prominent.
'the word will not surface' — rise into consciousness, as a submarine surfaces; suffice = be enough.
'it arises about twice a week' — comes into being that often; arouse = awaken a feeling.
'the retrieval fails partially' — only partly, since the meaning arrives but the sound does not; presumably = probably.
'psychologists model the dictionary as partly split' — represent it in theory; meddle takes 'in'.
'the gap between the two, yawning open' — gaping like a chasm; yank = pull sharply.
'stubbornly uncooperative' — refusing to work with you; unprovoked = happening without cause.
'thinking of something else entirely' — 'something else' is the fixed pattern; 'something other' does not stand alone here.
